"These things have I spoken unto you, being with you. But the Comforter, which is the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you," John 14:25 and 26. Go on to read Acts 2:1-4; 3:1 to 4:31; Galatians 5:19-25 and you will have the Scripture passages for Sunday's lesson, with Ephesians 1:3-14 as the devotional reading.


PETER ACTS BRAVELY


IN the passage in Acts we have the picture of Peter and John about to enter the temple on the Sabbath, when suddenly they find themselves confronted by a sick beggar. What could they do with him and for him? He was asking for money.


Peter said, "Silver and gold have I none, but such as I have give I thee, In the Name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk!"


The lame man stood up, leaping and walking and rejoicing, and went into the temple with Peter and John. Only the power of God can do such mighty works. Peter was not afraid to tackle the man's needs, since he relied upon God's wisdom and strength.


WHY PETER WAS BRAVE


PETER is often pictured as a very quick-tempered person. He was usually the first to speak in every situation. He was the leader of the group—a natural leader of men. But Peter did not assume to meet the poor man's need in his strength. Only "in the Name of Jesus."


When we forget self and rely upon the Holy Spirit for direction, we are enabled to meet and master any situation. Juniors will do well to remember these words, "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith the Lord of hosts" Zechariah 4:6.


Junior boys and girls can meet life's tasks in the same assurance in which Peter dealt with the lame man, if we rely upon the Holy Spirit.


SECRET OF CHRISTIAN POWER


"You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you" Acts 1:8. That is the secret of the Christian's power. It does not originate elsewhere. It is God's gift to those who implicitly trust in him.


This great truth is particularly appealing to intermediates and seniors. Young people are keenly sensitive to the times in which they live. We live today in an hour of unprecedented power—atomic energy! But all of the marvels of modern science have not been able to give young people the sense of mastery. Rather, we are afraid. The scientists themselves tell us that this is history's most precarious age.


Only when the Holy Spirit is regnant in our hearts do we possess the power of which Paul is writing in Galatians, when he says, "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long suffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance."


WHEN WE HAVE THAT POWER


Why, then, should we ever be weak, when we may avail that power? This is the most searching question for any Christian. The answer will lead us to certain inevitable admissions. We become weak spiritually when we forget to pray, when we forget to read God's word, when we allow the interests of this world to blind our eyes and deafen our ears to the reality of God's presence.


The Holy Spirit will dwell with us, if only we will welcome him. He will not come unbidden; he will not remain unwanted. He cannot be made secondary. Either he guides or surrenders the rein to us.


Our lives are spiritually strong and healthy when the Holy Spirit governs. Our work is effective, our words are compelling. We speak not in our wisdom, but the wisdom of God. We go not in our strength, but in His strength.

parts of the Red empire, has loud
speaker in the market place or on
government buildings and the peo-
ple are compelled to gather daily to
hear the broadcasts. But all they
get is government propaganda,
which paints in the darkest colors
the men who govern the Western
world.


The Soviet press, which is far
more widely distributed and read
than in the days of the Czar, con-
tains nothing but the views of the
Kremlin. Any slight departure from
the prescribed party line by the
government officials who call them-
selves reporters and editors is
severely punished.


In the United States and other
Western countries the Communists
and other willing or unwilling tools
of Moscow can express themselves
freely. This is not, however, the
case in the U. S. S. R., where not a
single person dares, or has the op-
portunity, to say a single good word

tain.

papers and magazines which strict-

Henry A. Wallace in the United
States and Communist leaders in
Western Europe—who are free to
repeat to their followers over the
radio ideas which emanate directly
from Moscow. Those ideas could
not be heard otherwise by millions
of Western peoples who do not have
short-wave sets.

Street. By strange coincidence,
on September 2, the Moscow ra-
dio, commenting on the American
election, stated: "The Wall Street
monopolists know that candidates
of both Republican and Democratic
Parties voice their policies."

get to the Russian people them-
selves the chances of another world
conflagration could be greatly di-
minished. But unfortunately there
is no way to get to those kindly and
simple people until their present
regime is overthrown.


The more than 190,000,000 in-
habitants of the U. S. S. R., domi-
nated by some 2,500,000 well-armed
and skillful secret policemen, can-
not rise and free themselves of
their government, which is a night-
mare not only to the rest of the
world, but to the Russian people
themselves.

cal disturbances, is just the place
for quiet vacation, says Ruth
Rose, screen writer and former ac-
tress.


Miss Rose is here for the filming
of her latest story, "Mr. Joseph
Young of Africa" based on the per-
sonal experiences of herself and her
husband, Ernest Beaumont Schoeds-
ack. Mr. Schoedsack is directing
the picture with Merian C. Cooper.


She says she has no patience with
Americans who yearn to see India,
Australia, South America or some
other far-off land, but hesitate be-
cause the times are troublesome.


Why don't they go, if they really
want to? The trains and boats are
still running," she declared.


Miss Rose's screen plays include
"King Kong," "Range and Lives
of Bengal Lancer." "King Kong"
was written in collaboration with
James Creelman from an original
story, "Kong," by Cooper and the
late Edgar Wallace.


When Miss Rose left the New
York stage 20 years ago she joined
South American expedition search-
ing for rare birds and insects. Two
marine expeditions to the Galapa-
gos Islands followed, on the second
of which she met and married Mr.
Schoedsack. They travelled together
in India, Sumatra and Africa.


Miss Rose wants to go back to
India. But Mr. Schoedsack, some-
what to her surprise, is finding Hol-
lywood sufficiently exciting.

Members of American Legion
Post 113 voted at the regular
meeting, Oct. 21, to open the club
rooms more often so members
may enjoy the facilities.


The post will hold open house
Saturday, Oct. 80, for Legion
naires and their friends. Ar
rangements for this party are un-
der the direction of Arthur Rich
ards. Admission free. Dancing,
cards, refreshments. If this party
proves successful it will be con-
tinued every Saturday night. If
demand later warrants it the Le-
gion hall will be opened other
nights in the week. The long
range plan is to make the Le-
gion hall a club room and recrea-

who are seeking benefits by dishonest means.
We should, for example, lengthen interviewing
time to permit us to ferret information in
sufficient detail to determine whether the
claimant is making dishonest representations
in order to get unemployment benefits. Suf-
ficient administrative funds would permit us to
review thoroughly the claimants' records for
contradictory statements and to institute im-
mediate "follow-up" action in all questionable
cases. There are many other steps, fraud
deterrents in themselves, which could be taken
but these would require considerably more
money to administer.

District employers have a sal responsibility
in this program. It is to their advantage to
cooperate fully with the board in order to
protect the money they have contributed to
the local unemployment fund. The
board's regulations require employer to
submit a separation report within 48 hours
after a worker leaves his employ. This sep-
aration report tells us when employee was
separated, and why he was separated. If the
report indicates the employee was discharged
for misconduct, voluntarily and without good
cause, or was directly involved in a strike or
labor dispute, an automatic disqualification
could be imposed as provided by the law. It
is regrettable that almost 50 percent of local
employers fail to comply with the provisions
of the regulations requiring them to send us
separation reports, and constantly permit
claimants to receive benefits which they should
be disqualified.

Employers can further assist and protect
their own interests as well, by pairing and
giving employees a "Low Earner Report"
whenever workers are employed less than full
time during any week; by verifying workers'
Social Security numbers and date of employ-
ment before submitting wage reports; by
promptly reviewing and replying to notices
sent them by our office; and by reporting any
misrepresentation made by an employee or
former employee involving unemployment
benefit rights.

distinction must be made between deliberate
dishonesty and innocent mistakes made by
claimants because of the complexity of the
law. As mentioned before, we deal here
only with fraud that is knowingly committed
by claimants. It is my considered opinion that
"willful" fraud is involved in relatively few
of the total applications filed for unemp-
loyment benefits. However, there are some cas-
es. And we must and will continue to do every-
thing administratively possible to stamp them
out.

Here is a partial solution to this problem of
willful fraud. The use of an accession or a
separation report in every instance. Is it
the cure? I don't know. Furthermore, I
would pay the bill for this additional work.
The boss. It might be well for me to add that
there has never been and will never be
a law or regulation written which would make
an intentionally dishonest person honest. Un-
fortunately, we will always have thieves,
murderers, and a few just-plain dishonest
people.

A recent analysis of benefit payments made
by this board reveals that:

The lowest average check for any year
was $1921.

The highest average check for any year
was $1769.

The average check for the entire period since
the inception of the law, is $1929.

For two years, the average duration of claim
was only 8 weeks.

The longest average duration, for one year,
was 1871 weeks.

And the average duration for the entire
period—109 weeks.

These figures clearly indicate that there has
not been too much chiseling by District em-
ployees under this program, but we must strive
to eliminate the few chiselers without establishing
unreasonable restrictions affecting the gre-
at majority of honest and deserving claimants.
We are engaged in the administration of
employee legislation, and the workingman is
urgently requested to cooperate with the pro-
gram officials, and with his employer to prevent the
undermining or abuse of this, one of the most
valuable and important programs established
for his economic security.

There was a time, in this country, when even a whole day
OF life was not taken for granted; much less water, shelter, a safe
nights sleep. Now, by reason of a uniquely bountiful heritage, we
take for granted : too much. We assume. Expect. Insist. Nowhere
else in the world is this possible.


Unthinking, we accept not only the great urgencies of food,
shelter and clothes but the whole spate of little things that make
APP a way of life, a pattern of security. We take for granted the
protection of our locked front door; a roof to our living room;
heat, lights. We expect our children, bursting with vitality and
ytamln b, to knock our hats askew with the vigor of their well
come. AS breathing, we take for granted a hot bath, soap, PENCIL
lin, sodas at the corner drug store.


We assume that young husbands will make a successful
future for themselves, that older husbands will retire on what,
over the long years, they have put away. We expect our daughters
to have an evening dress. We cheerfuly assume that some decent
men will get voted into public office, We know that veterans can
get a CT loan, and assume that, with it, one of them will start a
future .. S. Steel Another will marry, and produce an Edison, a
Jefferson, a Carver. We take for granted that we will not be shot,
imprisoned, or have our everything" confiscated; that our child
rem will live to grow up.


What we forget every day, every moment, is our own his
tory. That it was not entirely to give us these luxuries-become-
necessities that men stayed on at Valley Forge for % cents a day;
that Lincoln did the fine, unpopular thing, unwaveringly; that
over $4,000 men died in prison camps between 81 and '64; that,

not to guarantee us ice cream and radios that women bore child

sweep to the West.


1t is good to remember what simple right to vote cost
other human beings. Perhaps they had no thought of us; they were
concerned with making their America. What they made is what
we have. To take this heritage, unthinkingly, for granted is a
first step to losing it.

Peters, secretary-treasurer of the group. The board plans to sell building and improvement bonds in $100 denominations in order to build their fund.
